title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 (computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5)). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap labeled exploratory per preregistration and interpreted cautiously given only four discordants). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the originally preregistered Bonferroni familywise multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests) could not be applied. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting, and provide artifact pointers and representative hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction:
Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Modern LLMs show promise for translating human intent to device configuration, yet hallucination and factual errors remain central reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and—if verification fails—run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload?

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts and deterministic adjudication. (2) Artifact‑grounded clarification of verifier semantics, execution accounting, and exact inferential computations so results are reproducible from the archived CSV/JSON artifacts. (3) Reconciliation of the preregistered exact conditional McNemar decision rule and an exploratory paired bootstrap description, with an explicit small‑discordant‑count caveat. (4) Operationally focused discussion of verifier blind spots, cost/latency tradeoffs, and the consequences of the unexecuted templated comparator for multiplicity control.
sections.related_work:
Three literatures motivate the study. First, surveys and system papers document active interest in LLMs for intent translation, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration while emphasizing hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers [doi:10.1145/3718958.3750537; https://openalex.org/W4411735779]. Intent‑driven configuration prototypes typically pair generators with ad‑hoc validation or operator oversight rather than large, controlled trials against deterministic verifiers [doi:10.1002/nem.2313].

Second, methodological work advocates explicit generate‑validate‑repair evaluation practices and standardized validator semantics; these works call for preregistered paired designs, verifier codebooks, and cost accounting for tool orchestration [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Our preregistered paired plan and archived artifacts respond directly to these methodological recommendations.

Third, deterministic configuration verifiers and scalable verifier systems show that many syntactic/workflow properties are automatically checkable, but verifier coverage varies and typically excludes control‑plane timing and vendor‑specific execution semantics [https://openalex.org/W4413757123]. We use a verifier that enforces canonical parsing, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, and paired‑field dependencies—properties commonly modeled by verification systems—while acknowledging its modeling limits.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N=500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). The preregistered primary decision rule is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as descriptive.

Generation and orchestration. For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini. The generation settings recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) are: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; temperature = null (recorded as null in the artifact); reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false. The GVR controller validates the shared candidate using deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification fails the controller issues at most one repair prompt to the same model (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline accepts the shared candidate without repair.

Deterministic verifier semantics and codebook. The primary verifier implements: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization, (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change patterns), (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups), (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields), and (v) final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome; for each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and boolean valid. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) and its artifact entry are enumerated in the archived execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and retrievable from the evidence bundle; the execution manifest contains the full hash manifest for codebook retrieval.

Provider‑call accounting and provider_call_audit clarification. Reviewers noted ambiguity in a provider audit field that lists "condition_counts": {"shared": 500, "guarded": 4}. To clarify (and citing the archived reconciliation artifact analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, SHA‑256 = 48bafa8c94272b409a7329e4946995f633a5de7789e5a96fdcef72d3bb127ffe): the reconciliation's provider_call_audit records hosted_model_call event counts broken down by logical stage names, not by per‑condition episode totals. In this run the two stage names are shared_initial_generation (500 calls) and repair (4 calls). The reconciliation artifact's "condition_counts" entry reports the stage counts keyed by short stage names (shared → 500 shared_initial calls; guarded → the 4 explicit repair‑stage calls). The reconciled provider audit also records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, and cache_miss_count = 504, consistent with 500 initial generations plus 4 repair calls; these fields and their hashes are archived in the evidence bundle (see deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA above and execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA fe9b93ef5c...).

Repair policy and logging. If the verifier fails the shared candidate the controller issues at most one minimal repair prompt that includes the original intent, the violation codes and short descriptions, and a constrained request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. A repair candidate is accepted only if it passes the verifier. All repair invocations and accept/reject outcomes are recorded per episode in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02) and in provider traces; the reconciliation artifact enumerates stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 500, "repair": 4}.
sections.results:
Execution totals and contingency. The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504 (execution manifest). analysis/condition_summary.csv (SHA‑256 = f3e197425cc03dec41cda77f078f6d0b079b06bbde7ac736de5fe988b027ac58) reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece) is: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates and all four repair attempts resulted in subsequent verifier passes; these four repaired episodes correspond to the observed discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008.

Exact conditional McNemar and numeric reproducibility. The preregistered conditional exact McNemar conditions on the observed discordant total n = n10 + n01 and computes the two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 under Binomial(n, 0.5). With n = 4 and k = 4 the one‑sided binomial tail PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16. The two‑sided p reported is p = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125 (clipped ≤1.0). The exact contingency CSV and analysis log (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 261ec80ea9343fccbcd0a62294f5382773770fd59d387dc9d749de50ca909b3e) permit reproduction of the p‑value and the bootstrap procedure (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000).

Exploratory paired bootstrap. The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016]; artifacts analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl record the bootstrap parameters and seed. We emphasize that the bootstrap was predeclared exploratory and that percentile CIs can have fragile coverage with tiny discordant counts (n = 4), which explains why the bootstrap interval can exclude zero even when the conditional exact McNemar is non‑significant. We therefore treat the bootstrap interval as descriptive.

Concise summary of repaired episodes (artifact‑grounded). The four repaired episodes are recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef5c...). In aggregate these four repairs addressed verifier‑detectable sequence or availability violations (examples: required ordering of make‑before‑break uplink switchover, required shutdown→change→restore sequences for MTU/VLAN changes). All four repairs produced subsequent verifier passes and correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). For auditors: the per‑episode scoring JSON objects and repair provider traces that enumerate exact violation codes and repair prompts are archived under execution/scoring/ and in execution/raw_results.jsonl; the execution manifest lists the exact artifact paths and the full hash manifest for codebook retrieval.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational meaning. The GVR pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest LLM overhead (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). Under the preregistered conditional exact McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but is fragile given only four discordants; because the conditional McNemar was preregistered as the primary decision rule we follow it for confirmatory claims.

Provider audit semantics and practical accounting. We clarified that the reconciliation's "condition_counts" reflect stage counts (shared_initial_generation vs repair) rather than per‑condition episode counts; the full provider_call_audit and reconciliation JSON (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; SHA‑256 = 48bafa8c...) contain the audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 500, "repair": 4}. These reconciled counts match the invocation accounting in the execution manifest and enable per‑accepted‑change cost estimates reported above.

Verifier coverage and limits. The deterministic verifier enforces canonical parsing, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency rules, and final‑state comparisons. These checks detect a broad class of syntactic and workflow errors captured by our synthetic grammar and were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes. The verifier does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane convergence timing, execution‑time exceptions, or hardware resource constraints; passing the verifier is therefore necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient to guarantee production safety. Expanding verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators) is required before production automation.

Consequences of the unexecuted templated comparator. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (the second confirmatory test H2) was not executed in this archived run; consequently the preregistered Bonferroni familywise correction across the two confirmatory tests cannot be applied. We therefore report the exact conditional McNemar p = 0.125 for the primary GVR vs LLM‑only comparison without applying the preregistered multiplicity adjustment. This limitation is explicitly documented in the Methods, Results, and Disclosure Statement and is recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (which was not executed here). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; key artifact hashes are quoted below in the Disclosure Statement.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
